extracted.intended_audience: literary scholars, narratology students, and creative-writing instructors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and conceptual distinctions for analyzing and composing narrative voice: temporal relation of narrating to story (subsequent/prior/simultaneous/interpolated), the balance between story and discourse, narrating duration, and nested narrative levels (extradiegetic/diegetic/metadiegetic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of narrating by temporal relation
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrating may be subsequent (telling after the events), prior (prophetic or predictive in relation to the narrated events), simultaneous (narrating contemporaneous with the action, often present tense), or interpolated (narration inserted between moments of the action).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each type has characteristic effects: interpolated narration is often complex because it involves multiple narrating instances and can entangle story and narrating; simultaneous narration tends to eliminate temporal interval and can either favor story-transparency or emphasize discourse (see examples: epistolary/journal forms, Jocabel's dream in Moyse sauve).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpolated narrating complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpolated narrating (narration that takes place between moments of action) is a priori the most complex, involving several narrating instances and the possibility that narrating affects the plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particularly intricate in epistolary novels with multiple correspondents where the letter is both medium and plot element (example: Les Liaisons dangereuses). Journals can loosen into monologue with indefinite temporal position (example: L'Etranger), producing uncertainties that resist simple analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of simultaneous (present-tense) narrating
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of the present tense brings narrating and story into rigorous simultaneity, eliminating temporal interval between them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This can produce two opposite results depending on emphasis: (1) if behaviorist/objective, it yields apparent objectivity and 'transparency' of narrative (e.g., early Robbe-Grillet, 'objective literature'); (2) if emphasis is on inward speech, it foregrounds narrating/discourse (interior monologue), reducing action to pretext (examples: Dujardin, Beckett, Claude Simon). Small shifts in emphasis can tip the narrative toward story or discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior (predictive) narrating and its placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Predictive or prophetic narrating (narrating that projects into the future of the story) occurs but is rarer in the corpus and often appears on a second, embedded level of narration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Aaron's prophetic narrative and Jocabel's premonitory dream in Moyse sauve; these are predictive relative to the immediate narrating instance but not necessarily relative to the ultimate implied author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subsequent narrating and the 'atemporal' narrating instance
rubrics_metrics.description: Most narratives are subsequent: the narrator tells after the events, usually via a past tense which often marks an indeterminate, ageless past; fictive narrating is typically presented as instantaneous and without measurable duration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although real writing may take years (Flaubert, Proust), the fictive narrating in the final text behaves as if it were a brief, atemporal moment. Analysts must note this paradox when mapping real genesis onto the final text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tense and aspect as signals of narrating/story relation
rubrics_metrics.description: Linguistic choices (preterite, passé composé, present) carry different temporal connotations: e.g., the French passé composé connotes relative closeness; the epic preterite may be argued to have no temporal value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of present can disclose relative contemporaneity; choice of tense interacts with narrative effects (vividness, proximity, historicity). See references to Benveniste on passé composé, and debates like Kate Hamburger on the 'epic preterite'. Examples: L'Etranger owes much to tense choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final convergence / temporal isotopy between story and narrating
rubrics_metrics.description: When the temporal distance between story-time and narrating-time shrinks (often toward the end of a long narrative), story and narrating can approach isotopy: the story 'overtakes' the narrating, producing denouement effects or seeming convergence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First-person narratives commonly show final convergence (narrator = character who recounts), but the interval may remain conceptually nonzero (asymptote). Examples: Robinson Crusoe paradigm; Madame Bovary, Eugenie Grandet, and modern long narratives; Proust's Recherche resists full merging of hero and narrator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrating duration versus writing duration (fictional instantaneousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The fictive narrating instance in the text is often represented as instantaneous (a 'moment brief as a flash of lightning'), even when the real writer spent years composing the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysts should register shifts and discordances that arise from the actual genesis of the work (e.g., Proust's shifting 'today' as he wrote over years) but treat the narrating instance in the final text as a single moment without duration, except where the text explicitly marks duration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focalization through narrator versus hero (closely allied instances)
rubrics_metrics.description: When narrating instance and hero coincide closely (e.g., journals, letters), focalization through the narrator is simultaneously focalization through the hero, producing subtle dissonances between immediate impressions and later reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Cecile Volanges' letter where the Cecile of yesterday is seen by the Cecile of today; this displacement allows ironic counterpoints and the 'tiniest temporal interval' exploited by eighteenth-century novels (Pamela to Obermann).

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative levels: extradiegetic, diegetic, metadiegetic
rubrics_metrics.description: Events recounted in a narrative lie at a diegetic level immediately higher than the level of the narrating act producing that narrative. The first (frame) narrative's narrating instance is extradiegetic; a narrative contained within it is intradiegetic; a narrative inside that is metadiegetic, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map narrating instances and characters by level: e.g., M. de Renoncourt's Memoires (extradiegetic), Des Grieux's telling at the Lion d'or (intradiegetic), Des Grieux's own narrated loves (metadiegetic). The terms designate relative situations/functions, not permanent attributes of individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level-status independent of 'real' versus 'fictive' existence
rubrics_metrics.description: Level assignment (extradiegetic/diegetic/metadiegetic) does not depend on the 'real' or fictional existence of entities; fictive authors can be extradiegetic and real historical persons can be diegetic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the Marquis de Renoncourt is a fictive extradiegetic author addressing a public; Paris and Balbec may occupy the same narrative level even if one is real and the other fictional. Do not conflate extradiegetic with historical reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode of intradiegetic narration (oral/written/inward/nonverbal/iconographic)
rubrics_metrics.description: An intradiegetic second-degree narration can be oral, written, inward (dream or recollection), or nonverbal (an iconographic document that a narrator converts into narrative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the Curious Impertinent found in a cloakbag (Don Quixote) as a literary text within the text; Jocabel's dream as inward narration; Adrienne's song episode in Sylvie as 'memory half dreamed'; pictorial tableaux described by a character (Moyse sauve). Consider whether the second narrative is presented as transcribed, edited, or merely reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistolary and diary forms: audience, editorship, and live/prerecorded mixture
rubrics_metrics.description: Diaries and epistolary novels may not be addressed to a public and their fictive 'authors' often function as 'editors' rather than authors; epistolary/journal forms combine 'live' (immediate) and 'prerecorded' (after-the-event) modes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat letters/diaries as differentially aimed: some (Pamela, Werther, Obermann) are 'epistolary monodies' with an implied receiver; others (diaries) may have no intended public. These forms can create hybrid focalization (quasi-interior monologue vs account after the event) and affect how much narrating is presumed to be written/spoken/transcribed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of metadiegetic narrative as a structural technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Embedding narratives within narratives (metadiegesis) is a long-standing epic and novelistic device used to structure complex accounts and to manage perspectives and temporal relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical provenance: Odyssey (Ulysses' account to Phaeacians), Thousand and One Nights, Baroque novels (Astree) and later novel traditions. When composing or analyzing, consider how embedded narratives frame, justify, or problematize the primary narrative and how they instantiate levels.
